1. Introduction
CO2 electroreduction (CO2ER) to chemi-
cals and fuels by renewable electricity is 
a promising strategy to cope with climate 
change and fossil fuel depletion crisis.[1–4]  
In the electrolysis process, hydrogen 
evolution overwhelms CO2 reduction and 
therefore highly efficient electrocatalysts 
are required to regulate the competition 
between hydrogen evolution and CO2 
reduction.[5–7] Development of nonnoble 
metal catalysts is essential for large-
scale applications and transition metals 
are of great potential as catalysts for 
CO2ER.[8,9] Of transition metals, Cu and 
post-transition metals (Pb, Sn, In, Bi) are 
promising materials, primarily because 
of Cu’s low cost, high abundance, and 
catalytic activity and the post-transition 
metals’ high overpotentials of H2 evolu-
tion.[10] Among these four post-transition 
metals, Pb exhibits
sections.results:
Annealing treatment for Cu particles and 
commercial Cu foils is highly efficient to pro-
duce Cu nanostructures.[21,35,36] In this study, 
nickel foam (NF) was employed as a 3D 
framework substrate because of its large spe-
cific surface area, exceptional mechanical and thermal strength. 
Cu was electrochemically deposited on the NF and then 
annealed in air at 500 °C followed by electrochemical reduction 
of the resultant Cu oxides. As such, Cu NWs with diameters 
of 200–400 nm were densely grown on the porous Ni skeleton 
(Figure 1a,b). The electrodeposition of Pb on the surface of Cu 
NWs produced clusters of irregularly and unevenly distributed 
polygonal Pb particles (labeled Pbed/Cu NWs, see Figure 1c,d). 
Upon annealing at 300 °C in air and electrochemical reduction, 
the irregular polygonal structures were transformed into NPs 
of 5–10 nm, which were uniformly distributed on the surface of 
Cu NWs (labeled Pbar/Cu NWs, see Figure 1e,f). The transmis-
sion electron microscope (TEM) characterization (Figure 1g,h) 
shows that the lattice distance in shell area is 0.310  nm, 
representing the (111) plane of Pb2O (PDF#75-0201), which 
was due to the oxidation of lead by air dur
sections.conclusion:
3D hierarchical nanostructures of Cu–Pb electrocatalysts for 
high-performance CO2 reduction have been susscesfully pre-
pared by EAE on NFs. Cu was electrodeposited onto Ni foams 
in 0.5  m CuSO4 and 1.0  m H2SO4 solutions and subsequent 
annealing treatment at 500  °C followed by electroreduction 
in 0.5  m KHCO3 solution produced Cu NWs of 200–400  nm 
diameter. Pb clusters were then electrodeposited onto the Cu 
NWs and uniformly re-distributed in particle sizes of 5–10 nm 
by annealing treatment. The preparation procedure is simple 
and straightforward in producing hierarchical nanostruc-
tures of Cu–Pb bimetal catalysts. FEs of 19.2%, 50.6%, and 
22.0% for H2, CO, and HCOOH with a total current density 
of −9.35 mA cm−2 at −0.93 V versus RHE were obtained by the 
Cu–Pb catalyst with Pb decoration of 30 C. The CO/H2 ratios 
were in the range of typical syngas for industrial Fischer–
Tropsch synthesis. The use of Ni foams as porous 3D sub-
strates through electrodeposition and annealing treatment is of 
great potential to tune the catalytic activity of bimetal catalysts 
for efficient electroreduction of CO2.

Symmetry-breaking synthesis of colloidal nanocrystals with desired structures 
and properties has aroused widespread interest in various fields, but the 
lack of robust synthetic protocols and the complex growth kinetics limit their 
practical applications. Herein, a general strategy is developed to synthesize 
the Au–Cu Janus nanocrystals (JNCs) through the site-selective growth of Cu 
nanodomains on Au nanocrystals, which is directed by the substantial lattice 
mismatch between them, with the assistance of judicious manipulation of the 
growth kinetics. This strategy can work on Au nanocrystals with different archi-
tectures for the achievement of diverse asymmetric Au–Cu hybrid nanostruc-
tures. Of particular note, the obtained Au nanobipyramids (Au NBPs)-based 
JNCs facilitate the conversion of CO2 to C2 hydrocarbon production during elec-
trocatalysis, with the Faradaic efficiency and maximum pa
sections.results:
Scheme 1a illustrates the site-selective growth process of a Cu 
nanodomain on the side surface of a Au NBP to produce the Au 
NBP–side Cu JNCs (Au NBP–Cu JNCs). Each Au NBP featuring 
a fivefold rotational symmetry structure and consisting of two 
base-stacked pentagonal pyramids[50] is utilized as the seed. The 
crystalline structure of a Au NBP is depicted in Figure S1, Sup-
porting Information, with each NBP being encapsulated with 
10 facets.[51,52] The side facets are stepped periodically along the 
length direction to form the high-index {116} facets.[50,51] Cu 
atoms are expected to initially nucleate on one high-index {116} 
facet, because the Au atoms at the steps are generally coordi-
nately unsaturated and are more active for the nucleation of 
Cu (Scheme 1a, the first step). Due to the considerable lattice 
mismatch (≈11.4%) between Au and Cu,[49] the growth of Cu on 
the Au NBPs prefers to adopt the classic Volmer–Weber model 
through a 3D island growth (Scheme 1a, the second step).[49,53]

sections.conclusion:
In summary, a facile and general wet-chemistry method is 
developed for the synthesis of spatially separated Au NBP–Cu 
hybrid nanostructures on the basis of a large lattice mismatch 
between them. The concentrations of CTAB and HDA play 
crucial roles in the overgrowth of Cu nanodomains on the Au 
NBPs and determine the morphology of the Au–Cu nanostruc-
tures. The proposed synthesis method can be simply extended 
to other Au nanocrystals from 0D to 2D, enabling the produc-
tion of diverse asymmetric Au–Cu nanostructures. In addition, 
the spatial-separation design of the Au–Cu heterostructure

and selectivity of C2 production. The optimal FE value and 
maximum partial current density of the Au NBP–Cu JNCs are

defect density, and increased surface electrons is synthesized via a scalable 
plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition method, together with a postsyn-
thesis Ar-plasma treatment (VG-Ar). Subsequently, Cu@CuxO nanoparticles are 
deposited onto VG-Ar (Cu/VG-Ar) through a galvanostatic pulsed electrodeposi-
tion method. These Cu@CuxO nanocatalyst systems exhibit a superior elec-
trochemical CO2 reduction performance when compared to Cu-based catalysts 
supported on commercial graphene paper or pristine VG without postsynthesis

sections.results:
The graphene materials before and after Cu electrodeposition 
were first characterized using SEM. As illustrated in Figure S1 
(Supporting Information), the GP shows a typical 2D layered 
structure, while the VG and VG-Ar materials exhibit vertically-
orientated 3D carbon structures. After the decoration of Cu 
nanoparticles via PED, the 2D graphene surface was covered 
by a dense layer of aggregated Cu species. In contrast, the Cu 
species deposited on VG materials were well-dispersed with the 
size ranging from 60 to 80 nm. The SEM images of VG and 
VG-Ar also demonstrate that the postsynthesis Ar-plasma treat-
ment was mild and did not damage the 3D porous structure 
of VG, which results in the same Cu nanoparticle morphology. 
This is further confirmed by the TEM images (Figure S2, Sup-
porting Information), demonstrating no obvious changes in the 
morphology and size of the Cu nanoparticles dispersed on the

CuBi2O4 microspheres were prepared via the hydrothermal 
reaction using the precursors of Cu(NO3)2 and Bi(NO3)3 (see Ex-
perimental for more details). Since the hydrothermal temperature 
and time had significant influences on the product morphology 
and composition, these two experimental parameters were first 
carefully explored. It was found that 100 oC and 36 h gave rise to 
the most uniform CuBi2O4 microspheres as shown in Figure 1a. 
Polyethylene glycol 400 (PEG 400) was added during the hydro-
thermal reaction and found to play an important role in facilitat-
ing the formation of the microstructure. 
To characterize the microstructure of CuBi2O4 microspheres, 
scanning electron microscope (SEM) imaging was performed. 
Figure 1a showed uniform CuBi2O4 microspheres prepared under

sections.conclusion:
In summary, we reported the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction 
catalyzed by bimetallic Cu-Bi with high activity and selectivity. The 
bimetallic Cu-Bi electrocatalyst was in situ prepared by reducing 
the CuBi2O4 microspheres, which were synthesized by the facile 
hydrothermal method. The in situ formed bimetallic Cu-Bi elec-
trocatalyst showed excellent electrocatalytic performance toward 
reducing CO2 to formate in 0.5 mol·L–1 NaHCO3 electrolyte. High 
Faradaic efficiency over 90% for formate was maintained in a wide 
potential range with a maximum Faradaic efficiency of ~95% at  
–0.93 V and a large HCOO– partial current density of 8.2 mA·cm–2 
at –1.03 V. Moreover, the bimetallic Cu-Bi catalyst was very stable 
and maintained high Faradaic efficiencies of ~95% for over 6 h. 
The superior electrochemical performance of the bimetallic Cu-Bi 
electrocatalyst rendered it an attractive candidate for CO2 elec-
troreduction.

Use of Cu and Cu+ is one of the most promising approaches for the produc-
tion of C2 products by the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) 
because it can facilitate CO2 activation and CC dimerization. However, the 
selective electrosynthesis of C2+ products on Cu0Cu+ interfaces is critically 
limited due to the low electrocatalytic production of ethanol relative to eth-

afford high ethanol productivity by the electrocatalytic CO2RR. The aerogel is 
synthesized by a simple chemical redox reaction of a precursor and a reducing 
agent. CO2RR results reveal that the Cu/Cu2O aerogel produces ethanol as the 
major product, exhibiting a Faradaic efficiency (FEEtOH) of 41.2% and a partial 
current density (JEtOH) of 32.55 mA cm−2 in an H-cell reactor. This is the best 
electrosynthesis performance for
sections.results:

Cu/Cu2O aerogel networks for the high production of C2 
products by electrocatalytic CO2RR. The Cu/Cu2O aerogel was 
prepared by a simple wet chemical redox reaction in an aqueous

1. Introduction
The carbon dioxide electro reduction 
reaction (CO2RR) is an effective strategy 
to produce fuels and chemical feedstocks 
using intermittent renewable electricity 
(solar and wind). Conducted under mild 
conditions, the research community is 
hopeful that as well as being effective, it 
will prove to be achievable as a sustain-
able chemistry, carbon-neutral strategy.[1] 
Because of the complexity and range of 
coupling processes between multiple 
protons and electrons, a multitude of 
possible CO2 reduction products (C1–C4 
and hydrogen [H2]) can be generated 
using various types of electrocatalysts.[2] 
To date, although carbon monoxide 
(CO),[3] formate (HCOOH),[4] C2H4,[5] and 
C2H5OH[6] are common and relatively 
well-established 
products,

sections.conclusion:
In conclusion, a facile seed-assisted strategy for preparing 
PVP-capped Cu NPs was developed. Through controllable 
regulation of the oxidization state of surface Cu atoms, a dis-
tinct difference in CO2RR performance was demonstrated for 
different amounts of PVP capping, with the NPs coated with a 
sufficient amount of PVP (SPVP-Cu NPs) catalyzing the pro-
duction of CH4 and those that were considered PVP-deficient 
(DPVP-Cu NPs) catalyzing C2+ production. In this system, the 
PVP polymer plays a very critical role in manipulating the 
chemical state of the surface Cu atoms. Our study provides 
a new reference for the construction of Cu NPs with well-
defined different oxidization states on gas diffusion electrodes 
suitable for commercial CO2RR systems to generate CH4 and 
C2+ products.

sections.conclusion:
In summary, we have developed an electron-deficient Cu3Ag1 
catalyst through interphase electron transfer strategy. The intro-
duction of Ag into Cu facilitated electron transfer from Cu to 
Ag, which generated electron-deficient Cu sites in the Cu3Ag1 
catalyst. DFT calculations confirmed that the electron-defi-
cient Cu sites particularly favored the adsorption of key ECR 
intermediates in the alcohol pathway such as CH3CHO* and 
CH3CH2O*. This finding was verified by the electrocatalytic

work has revealed the electron-deficient state of Cu atoms in 
Cu3Ag1 catalysts with ECR-to-alcohol selectivity and activity,

ABSTRACT: Highly porous 3D Cu skeletons (sponges)
modiﬁed by electropolishing, thermal annealing, and foam
electrodeposition have been studied as catalysts for the
electrochemical conversion of CO2 with a particular emphasis
on C2 products formation. These catalyst materials appear to
be promising for future applications where gaseous CO2

tuning the mean residence time of reaction intermediates

distribution. In particular, the annealed skeleton (300 °C, 12
h) and the one modiﬁed by Cu foam electrodeposition show
